projects.name: Provide food transfers to refugees
projects.description:
WFP, in collaboration with the Government of Angola and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), provided unconditional food transfers to 5,600 refugees (51 percent women and girls) from the Democratic Republic of Congo living in the Lóvua settlement in Lunda Norte province. This included 200 unregistered refugees who received assistance through the exceptional ration programme. WFP continued to provide reduced rations, meeting only 75 percent of the daily kilocalorie requirements due to persistent funding challenges. To mitigate supply chain disruptions caused by procurement delays, WFP increased efforts to source commodities locally.

WFP accompanied the food transfers with nutrition education to improve the knowledge about nutritious foods and support healthy behaviours. WFP, UNHCR, and partners also ensured ongoing nutrition screening, referrals, treatment, and follow-up for children diagnosed with acute malnutrition.
projects.outcome: The social protection system is strengthened to address vulnerabilities faced by Angolans across the life cycle and provide income security, particularly for children, women, persons with disabilities, persons in active age who are unable to earn sufficient income and older persons.

projects.name: Provide livelihood support to refugees and other crisis-affected populations to improve self-reliance
projects.description: In line with the joint livelihood strategy developed with UNHCR, WFP will continue to implement resilience and livelihood support activities, targeting over 1,200 refugees and host community members through the distribution of start-up kits and provision of equipment and training on different income-generating activities such as agriculture and beekeeping. Through the beekeeping project, launched with the support of José Eduardo dos Santos University, WFP aims to produce at least 20 metric tons of honey annually. Refugees also received conditional food transfers to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. WFP also plans to introduce other high-value chain production systems, such as fruit tree planting and fish farming, to help communities diversify their livelihoods and boost their income. In preparation, WFP, in collaboration with the Ministry of Fisheries, UNHCR, the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO), the Embassy of the Federative Republic of Brazil, and other partners, in 2024, organised a training on fish and fruit farming. Participants included host community members, members of the Association of Young Producers of Lunda Norte, technicians from the Provincial Directorates of Agriculture and Fisheries from Lunda Norte, and WFP staff. The training, which integrated theoretical lessons with practical activities and field visits, aimed to improve the knowledge and skills of participants and foster sustainable practices.

framework.name: Strategic Priority 1: PEOPLE - HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT
framework.description:
WFP focused on ensuring food insecure and shock-affected populations receive timely assistance to meet their basic food and nutrition requirements. WFP assists refugees and those affected by the drought in southern Angola, including children under five, primary school children, and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls (PBWG). WFP provides conditional and unconditional food transfers, school meals, and nutrition treatment integrated nutrition support. WFP also started a community and household asset creation intervention for a limited number of refugees to reduce their dependency on food assistance, build their capacity to rebuild livelihoods and boost resilience against economic shocks.

WFP assisted some 158,994 food-insecure and shock-affected populations (51 percent women) in meeting their urgent food and nutrition needs. WFP transferred over USD 2.9 million to beneficiaries through commodity voucher interventions and distributed 1,119 metric tons of food. The underachievement for both outputs can be explained by resource constraints with available funding covering only 67 percent of assessed needs, restrictions in the importation of certain food commodities, and prolonged supply chain processes. Due to these constraints, WFP was forced to cut food rations to refugees from 100 to 75 percent of the daily kilocalorie requirement, delay/suspend the implementation of certain activities and prioritise the most affected areas. When it comes to commodity voucher interventions, the planned needs were also linked to the drought response which was poorly resourced. WFP’s nutrition activities were particularly impacted by the long lead times for the procurement of specialized nutritious foods - Ready-to-Use Supplementary Food. 

 

In 2023, WFP continued to provide unconditional food transfers to refugees from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Due to the voluntary repatriation process in October 2023, the number of beneficiaries for this activity decreased slightly from 6,439 in 2022 to 6,092 in December 2023. This number includes approximately 200 vulnerable unregistered refugees who received assistance under the Exceptional Ration Programme[1]. Food transfers were accompanied by social behaviour change communication, including nutrition education and targeted messaging, to improve the knowledge about nutritious foods and support healthy food choices. In addition to sensitisation activities, WFP continued working with partners to ensure the availability of nutrition screening services and appropriate referrals and treatment of children diagnosed with acute malnutrition.

Despite WFP's assistance, the food security and nutrition situation in the Lóvua refugee settlement remains concerning. According to the Food Security Assessment conducted by WFP in May 2022, 9 out of 10 households continue to rely on food assistance as their primary source of food. The results from the Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) survey, conducted in August 2023, show a deterioration of the food security outcomes in comparison to 2022. The percentage of households with acceptable Food Consumption Score  decreased from 75 percent in December 2022 to 62 percent in August 2023. The reduced Coping Strategy Index (rCSI) also shows that close to 90 percent of surveyed households have used at least one food-based coping strategy in the last seven days before the survey. Compared with the PDM conducted in December 2022, the average rCSI has increased from 14.0 to 21.7. The deterioration of the situation can be explained by the reduction of the food ration, inconsistent distribution schedule, and the lack of availability of some food commodities to cover the monthly requirements of beneficiaries (due to long lead times and importation restrictions).

Given the high prevalence of food insecurity and dependence on WFP’s food assistance and considering that only a few voluntary repatriations are foreseen in the short and medium term, there is a pressing need to engage refugees in activities that will protect livelihood assets, rebuild self-reliance opportunities, and promote longer-term resilience. In line with the Joint Livelihood Strategy developed by WFP and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), WFP started a community and household asset creation project for a limited number of refugees. Under this activity, 644 beneficiaries received 35.6 metric tons of conditional food transfers, as well as agricultural inputs, and training opportunities on modern farming technologies, animal husbandry, and post-harvest management. A total of 125 beneficiaries from the host communities were also involved in the training activities and benefited from agricultural inputs. Targeted participants harvested around 43 metric tons of rice and vegetables which were used for household consumption and sold in local markets, thus contributing to increasing their income. The link between relief and resilience-building activities also helped to foster community ownership and collaboration and contributed to strengthening social cohesion and peaceful coexistence between refugees and host communities.

WFP is one of the eight partners who participate in the DRC Regional Refugee Response Plan. WFP and other development and humanitarian agencies cooperated through inter-agency coordination mechanisms established at the central and local levels to ensure a more coherent and effective response. WFP co-chaired the Food Security and Livelihoods Working Groups in Lunda Norte with UNHCR. WFP's Cooperating Partners – World Vision International (WVI) and the national non-governmental organization (NGO) Ajuda de Desenvolvimento de Povo para Povo, assisted with the distribution process and implementation of community and household asset creation activities, respectively.

For the drought response, together with the government and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), WFP provided integrated nutrition support to some 23,612 children under five [2] and 1,533 PBWG [3] for the prevention and treatment of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). In Namibe and Huíla provinces, WFP also provided commodity vouchers to the families of children diagnosed with MAM (around 92,000 beneficiaries) to increase recovery rates and improve household food security and nutrition outcomes. In coordination with the Ministry of Health, WFP trained 413 health centre staff and community workers (54 percent women) across five provinces on the management of acute malnutrition, including screening, active case finding, management, distribution of SNFs and counseling. WFP raised awareness about malnutrition among affected communities and health staff. WFP developed its nutrition programmes in line with the priorities and objectives defined by the National Nutrition Programme and the National Strategy for Food Security and Nutrition to promote national and local ownership and ensure a smooth handover of nutrition programmes.  

WFP continued the implementation of the emergency school feeding programme to support primary school children and their families during the lean season. Due to the lack of school infrastructure for warehousing and meal preparation, in January 2023, WFP started distributions of take-home rations (THR) for three months to ensure that all students and their families received assistance[4]. Some 7,330 beneficiaries were provided with THR, while 2,060 primary school children received hot meals[5],[6]. WFP sourced 30 percent of the food for the preparation of meals from local farmer associations which helped to enhance their access to local markets and boost local agriculture production. PDM data showed that enrolment increased by 28 percent. The retention rate remained high at 94 percent (above the 85 percent target). The results of the project (completed in April 2023) show that school feeding remains an effective mechanism for keeping children in school, increasing retention rates, and improving learning outcomes.

WFP also reached beneficiaries, parents and caregivers, both male and female, at the household and community level, in health facilities, schools, and food distribution points through information/awareness sessions, cooking demonstrations, and radio spots with nutrition messaging, and conducted regular refreshers for health professionals. Some 388,000 people[7] were reached through social behaviour change communication approaches.

In 2023, drought-response activities were implemented directly with the Government and WFP’s Cooperating Partners, WVI and Joint Aid Management International. Specifically, WFP worked with local authorities to ensure the exchange of knowledge and ensure a smooth handover process at the end of the projects. For the programmes on community-based management of acute malnutrition, WFP worked with the Provincial Departments of Health and Social Action, while the emergency school feeding programme was implemented in coordination with the Provincial Department of Education. WFP staff regularly reported to and coordinated with local stakeholders at regular provincial meetings to avoid duplication of efforts/geographic coverage areas, maximise opportunities for collaboration, and ensure synergies with other humanitarian and development programs. WFP actively participated in the work of the Humanitarian International Country Group to ensure a timely and coordinated response with other UN agencies and engaged government counterparts in all stages of implementation. WFP and UNICEF’s interventions converged geographically and programmatically, which contributed to optimizing resources and improving outcomes. The two agencies established a referral mechanism for children with acute malnutrition and joint community feedback mechanisms.

Gender and age were partially integrated into the implementation of the activities including through gender-separate focus group discussions and the analysis of the particular needs of households headed by women during post-distribution monitoring exercises to support evidence-based programming. WFP took into consideration the unique needs of women during distribution cycles and asset creation and livelihood activities. Women and youth representatives accounted for the majority of the members of the Food Management Committee in the Lóvua settlement. Women were also represented in the school management committees. This helped to ensure that women and young people had an equal voice in decision-making and equal access to resources and opportunities.
